title: Rohrdommel und Wiedehopf
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 173. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (muthig, übermüthig).
about: KHM 173 is another etiological tale in miniature: an old cowherd explains that the bittern's dull cry and the hoopoe's shrill one are what remains of two herdsmen, one who let his cattle graze on pasture so rich they grew wild and unruly, the other who drove his onto barren hills until they grew too weak to move. Neither herd would come home at evening, and the men's calls to them became the birds' cries forever after — a plain little parable about moderation.

sentences.t: „Wo weidet ihr eure Herde am liebsten?“ fragte einer einen alten Kuhhirten.
sentences.l: “Where do you like best to pasture your herd?” someone asked an old cowherd.
sentences.i: “Where do you most like to graze your herd?” a man asked an old cowherd.
sentences.n: “weidet” is from weiden, to pasture or graze (cattle); “ihr” is the plural, respectful “you” the stranger uses to the herdsman.

sentences.t: „Hier, Herr, wo das Gras nicht zu fett ist und nicht zu mager; es thut sonst kein gut.“
sentences.l: “Here, sir, where the grass is not too rich and not too lean; otherwise it does no good.”
sentences.i: “Here, sir, where the grass is neither too rich nor too lean; otherwise it does no good.”
sentences.n: “fett” (rich, fat) and “mager” (lean, poor) describe the pasture. “thut” is the 1857 spelling of tut (does); “kein gut” = kein Gutes, no good.
“der Herr” names the questioner, here “sir, the gentleman” — the same word that served a moment ago as the respectful address “Herr.”

sentences.t: „Hört ihr dort von der Wiese her den dumpfen Ruf?“ antwortete der Hirt, „das ist der Rohrdommel, der war sonst ein Hirte und der Wiedehopf war es auch.
sentences.l: “Do you hear the dull call there from the meadow?” answered the herdsman, “that is the bittern; he was once a herdsman, and the hoopoe was one too.
sentences.i: “Do you hear that hollow call over there from the meadow?” answered the herdsman; “that is the bittern — he was once a herdsman, and so was the hoopoe.
sentences.n: “sonst” here means “formerly, once,” not “otherwise.” Rohrdommel = the bittern, a marsh bird with a deep booming call; Wiedehopf = the hoopoe. The bird-names are glossed and left in the original.

sentences.t: Ich will euch die Geschichte erzählen.
sentences.l: I will tell you the story.
sentences.n: “will” is wollen (to want, to intend), not the English future auxiliary; “euch” is the plural, respectful “you.”

sentences.t: Der Rohrdommel hütete seine Herde auf fetten grünen Wiesen, wo Blumen im Überfluß standen, davon wurden seine Kühe muthig und wild.
sentences.l: The bittern pastured his herd on rich green meadows, where flowers stood in abundance; from that his cows grew spirited and wild.
sentences.i: The bittern grazed his herd on rich green meadows where flowers grew in plenty, and from that his cows became spirited and wild.
sentences.n: “davon” = “from that, thereby,” pointing back to the rich grass. “muthig” is the 1857 spelling of mutig (spirited, bold).

sentences.t: Der Wiedehopf aber trieb das Vieh auf hohe dürre Berge, wo der Wind mit dem Sand spielt, und seine Kühe wurden mager und kamen nicht zu Kräften.
sentences.l: The hoopoe, however, drove the cattle onto high barren hills, where the wind plays with the sand, and his cows grew lean and did not come to their strength.
sentences.i: The hoopoe, though, drove his cattle up onto high barren hills where the wind plays with the sand, and his cows grew lean and never gained their strength.
sentences.n: “zu Kräften kommen” is an idiom, to gain strength — literally “come to strengths.” “dürr” = barren, dry.

sentences.t: Wenn es Abend war und die Hirten heimwärts trieben, konnte Rohrdommel seine Kühe nicht zusammenbringen, sie waren übermüthig und sprangen ihm davon.
sentences.l: When it was evening and the herdsmen drove homeward, the bittern could not bring his cows together; they were over-spirited and sprang away from him.
sentences.i: When evening came and the herdsmen drove homeward, the bittern could not gather his cows; they were too frisky and bounded away from him.
sentences.n: “sprangen ihm davon” — the “ihm” is a dative of disadvantage, they sprang away “on him.” “übermüthig” (1857) = übermütig, high-spirited, unruly.

sentences.t: Er rief „bunt, herüm“ (bunte Kuh, herum), doch vergebens, sie hörten nicht auf seinen Ruf.
sentences.l: He called “Bunt, come round!” (dappled cow, come round), yet in vain; they did not heed his call.
sentences.i: He called “Bunt, round you come!” (dappled cow, round!) — but in vain; they paid no heed to his call.
sentences.n: The round-bracket gloss “(bunte Kuh, herum)” is the Grimms’ own, explaining the herdsman’s cry to their readers. “bunt” = dappled, many-coloured, here a cow-call; “herüm” is a dialect form of herum (round, back here).

sentences.t: Wiedehopf aber konnte sein Vieh nicht auf die Beine bringen, so matt und kraftlos war es geworden.
sentences.l: The hoopoe, however, could not bring his cattle onto their legs, so faint and strengthless had it grown.
sentences.i: The hoopoe, for his part, could not get his cattle onto their feet, so limp and strengthless had they grown.
sentences.n: “auf die Beine bringen” = to get onto their feet, rouse. “Vieh” (cattle) is grammatically singular, so “es” = “it,” though in English we say “they.”

sentences.t: „Up, up, up!“ schrie er, aber es half nicht, sie blieben auf dem Sand liegen.
sentences.l: “Up, up, up!” he shrieked, but it did not help; they stayed lying on the sand.
sentences.i: “Up, up, up!” he cried, but it was no use; they lay where they were on the sand.
sentences.n: “up” is Low German for auf (up, get up) — the hoopoe’s driving-cry. “es half nicht” = it did not help, to no avail.

sentences.t: So gehts wenn man kein Maß hält.
sentences.l: So it goes when one keeps no measure.
sentences.i: That is how it goes when one keeps no moderation.
sentences.n: “gehts” = geht es (it goes); “Maß halten” is to keep measure, to show moderation — the point of the tale.

sentences.t: Noch heute, wo sie keine Herde mehr hüten, schreit Rohrdommel „bunt, herüm,“ und der Wiedehopf „up, up, up!“
sentences.l: Even today, now that they tend no herd any more, the bittern cries “Bunt, come round,” and the hoopoe “Up, up, up!”
sentences.i: To this day, though they tend no herd any longer, the bittern cries “Bunt, round you come,” and the hoopoe “Up, up, up!”
sentences.n: An etiology: the birds’ present calls are told as the herding-cries left over from their human days. “noch heute” = even now, to this day.

glossary.herde: die Herde — herd, flock of cattle (NOT der Herd/hearth)
glossary.hört: hören — to hear (2nd pl.; hört ihr … = do you hear … — NOT hört auf/stops)
glossary.liebsten: lieb — am liebsten = most gladly, best (superlative adverb)
glossary.spielt: spielen — to play (3rd sg.; der Wind spielt mit dem Sand = the wind plays with the sand)
